# Percent of Spend Is a Conflict of Interest With a Logo on It.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-09 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Media agencies paid a percentage of spend earn more when clients spend more, not when the spending works. ANA research has documented rebates, principal-based markups and commissions that persist for media long after other services moved to fees. lowob runs media on three rules: a flat fee per account, no fronted spend, and fixed fees against written scope.

Most media agencies are still paid, in whole or part, as a percentage of what their clients spend. The agency's revenue goes up when spending goes up, not when spending works, so every recommendation about budget, channel or pace is made by a party paid more if the answer is "more." That is not an accusation of bad faith. It is a conflict of interest with a logo on it. The ANA's own research shows how the incentive plays out, and three rules remove it.

The arrangement is so common that it rarely gets examined. It is easy to administer, it scales with the account, and it sounds fair: the agency does more work when the budget is larger, so it earns more.

Look at it for one minute from the client's side and the problem is obvious. The agency's revenue goes up when the client's spending goes up. It does not go up when the spending works. Most people in the industry are trying to do good work inside a structure that rewards something else.

## How agencies are paid now

The industry has moved, but less for media than for anything else. The ANA's 18th Trends in Agency Compensation study, published in December 2022 from 101 client-side marketers covering 336 agency relationships, found 82% used fee-based compensation, up from 68% in 2016. Performance incentives were falling: 41% used them, down from 61% in 2013. Media was the exception. Only about half of ANA members paid media agencies by fee, the lowest of any service, and 19% still used commissions for media planning or buying, against 7% for agency services overall.

| Model | How the partner earns more | What it rewards | Who holds the risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Percentage of spend | The client spends more | Volume | The client |
| Hourly or labour-based fee | More hours are billed | Time | The client |
| Fronted spend with a margin | More media passes through the partner | Credit and control | Split, with the partner controlling the account |
| Principal-based (resold) media | The markup on inventory | Inventory the partner owns | The client, often without seeing the markup |
| Flat fee per account against written scope | The client hires them for the next account | Finishing the defined work | Shared, and visible |

## What the incentive produces

Percentage fees shape behaviour in ways that are easy to see once named.

Budgets rarely come down. When a channel is underperforming, the recommendation is to test more creative, not to pause. Cheap inventory is attractive because it inflates volume at the same fee rate. "Always-on" spending is defended on principle. Reports emphasise scale over outcomes. And the agency has little reason to tell a client that a channel is closed to their category, because a closed channel is budget that cannot be placed.

The evidence shows the incentive extends beyond the headline fee. In 2016 the ANA commissioned K2 Intelligence to investigate media buying in the US. From 150 sources, the report found cash rebates paid to agencies by media sellers based on spend, often without the advertiser knowing; rebates disguised as research or consulting fees; and principal-based buying, where the agency buys inventory for itself and resells it to the client, at markups ranging from about 30% to 90%. Some media buyers reported pressure to steer client spend toward that inventory. The study was not an audit, named no companies, and five of six major holding companies declined to make executives available. It is still the most detailed public account of how volume incentives travel through the system.

Cheap volume has a measurable cost too. In the ANA's 2023 programmatic study, made-for-advertising sites took 21% of impressions and 15% of spend, and the average campaign ran on about 44,000 domains. A fee calculated on spend is indifferent to which of those domains the money reached.

The alternative is to set the budget from the company's own unit economics, cost per qualified opportunity and payback, as our piece on [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) describes, so that the size of the spend is never the partner's call alone.

None of that requires anyone to be dishonest. It only requires people to respond to how they are paid.

> A fee structure is not a detail of the contract. It is the strongest predictor of the advice you will receive.

## Three rules that remove the conflict

We run media on three rules, and we publish them because they are the answer to the question every media buyer should be asking.

**A flat fee per account, never a percentage of spend.** The fee is for the work of running the account: setup, inventory standards, verification, optimisation, reporting. It is the same whether the client spends thirty thousand or three hundred thousand. The only way to earn more is to earn the next account, which happens when this one works.

**We never front media spend.** The client pays the platforms and partners directly, or funds a media account in their own name. The moment an agency lends money to buy media, it becomes a creditor with an interest in volume, and it gains control of the account history, pixel data and platform relationships that should belong to the client. On Google Ads, for example, if a manager account holds ownership of a client's account, its admins can change who has access to it.

**Fixed fee against written scope, never hourly.** The scope says what will be done, what will be delivered, how long it takes, and what it does not include. Hourly billing rewards slowness. A percentage rewards volume. A fixed fee against a written scope rewards finishing. The ANA's data shows the largest advertisers moving the same way: among those spending $500 million or more a year, 53% used fixed or output-based fees in 2022, up from 5% in 2016.

## How to ask for it

A client does not have to hire us to use this. Ask any media partner three questions.

1. **If I halve my budget next month, what happens to your fee?**
2. **Whose name is on the ad accounts, and who holds the pixel and conversion history if we part ways?**
3. **What is in scope, in writing, and what is excluded?**

Add a fourth if the plan includes programmatic: **do you, or any company you own, sell us inventory as principal, and do you receive rebates or volume incentives from sellers?** The K2 findings are why.

The answers tell you what the partner is actually selling. A partner paid a percentage is selling placement. A partner who fronts spend is selling credit. A partner paid hourly is selling time. A partner on a flat fee against written scope is selling the outcome of a defined piece of work, and can be judged on it. Our guides to [how marketing services are priced](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-services-are-priced/) and [pricing architecture for services firms](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-architecture-for-services-firms/) cover the wider fee landscape.

## The honest limit

Flat fees have a floor. Below a certain account size the work does not cover the fee, and a good partner will say so rather than take the account and under-serve it. That is why we publish a minimum and the next step in the same proposal: the client should always know what the engagement costs, what it includes, and what it would cost to go further, before anyone starts.

Flat fees also move a risk to the client: a partner paid the same regardless of spend has less reason to find more scale when scale is the right answer. Written scope and a quarterly review of what the account produced handle that. Our piece on [self-serve, managed desk or agency](https://lowob.com/research/self-serve-vs-managed-media/) covers when each model fits.

## lowob takeaways

- **Percentage fees pay for volume.** Every budget recommendation comes from a party paid more if the answer is "more."
- **The incentive travels.** Rebates and principal-based markups were documented by the ANA's own investigation.
- **Three rules remove it.** A flat fee per account, no fronted spend, fixed fees against written scope.
- **Ask before you sign.** What happens to the fee at half the budget, whose name is on the accounts, and what is in scope.
